analysis.one_liner: Sets federal child-safety standards for handguns, dealers, and gun storage, with grants for tracking and education.
analysis.headline: The Children's Gun Violence Prevention Act of 1999 drew 61 cosponsors — 55 Democrats and 6 Republicans — but died in House committees without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred the manufacture or import of handguns that fail a drop test or lack child-resistant triggers, banned selling semiautomatic assault weapons to minors, revoked the licenses of dealers who willfully sell guns to minors, required two forms of ID from buyers under 24, imposed safety and security standards on gun shops, and penalized adults who leave loaded firearms where children can reach them. It also funded state tracking of child gunshot injuries, school programs on gun violence prevention, and the expansion of federal gun-tracing efforts aimed at illegal trafficking to people under 24. The bill never got past committee referral in the House.
analysis.who_benefits: Children and families would gain protections against accidental shootings, access to guns by minors, and illegal gun trafficking; schools and state health departments would receive federal grant funding.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Children and families at risk of gun violence

how_it_helps.text: Bars manufacture or import of 'unsafe handguns' — those that fail a drop test, lack a child-resistant trigger for children under 5, lack a magazine disconnect safety, or lack an anti-theft/lock mechanism [S2] [S3].
Extends the existing juvenile handgun ban to semiautomatic assault weapons and doubles the prison term for arming a juvenile for a violent crime [S2] [S3].

Mandates automatic license revocation for dealers who willfully sell firearms to minors, two forms of ID for buyers believed under 24, and minimum safety and security standards for gun shops [S2] [S3].

Makes it a federal offense, with fines up to $10,000 and up to a year in prison, to leave a loaded firearm accessible to a juvenile without a locking device, with exceptions for self-defense and lawful use [S2] [S3].
Authorizes federal grants for state child firearm injury tracking, school gun-violence education programs, and expanded federal tracing of guns used by young people [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Handgun manufacturers would bear redesign costs to meet safety standards; gun dealers would face licensing consequences, inspection requirements, and compliance costs; adult gun owners could be penalized for unsafe storage.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun makers, dealers, and some owners

drawbacks.text: The 'unsafe handgun' definition could effectively ban many common handgun designs, since requiring magazine disconnect safeties and child-resistant triggers would force redesign of existing models rather than incremental safety changes [S2] [S3].

The storage mandate and dealer security standards impose costs on gun owners and small dealers, and opponents argued such federal standards overlap with existing state child-access-prevention laws [S3].

Critics of design mandates generally argued they do little to stop deliberate criminal use and add expense without proven benefit; the bill relied on agency rulemaking ('the Secretary shall determine') for many details [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's direct benefits to families — fewer child shootings from unlocked or unsafe guns, stricter dealer accountability, and funded prevention programs — were modest in scale but real. The costs fell on a specific, concentrated industry: manufacturers facing redesign requirements and dealers facing new standards and penalties. The design mandates were broad and delegated heavily to agency rulemaking, so opponents had a fair argument about compliance burden and scope; supporters would counter that drop-test failures and child access are documented causes of child deaths.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and their subcommittees in spring 1999, and none of them ever held a markup or advanced it, so it died when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001 [S1] [S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy introduced the bill on March 25, 1999 [S1] [S2].
It was referred to the Judiciary, Education and the Workforce, and Commerce committees [S5].
In April 1999 it was referred to subcommittees on Telecommunications, Trade and Consumer Protection; Health and Environment; Crime; and Early Childhood, Youth and Families [S5].
No hearing, markup, or floor action followed; the last recorded action after the referrals was the sponsor's introductory remarks on May 14, 1999 [S5].
The bill attracted 61 cosponsors, including 6 Republicans [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers and dealers avoided the new safety-design mandates, dealer licensing penalties, security standards, and inspection requirements the bill would have imposed. Children and families gained nothing, since none of the bill's protections took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun makers and dealers who faced no new rules

for.name: Rep. Carolyn McCarthy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on it.

for.name: 6 of 223 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it a small bipartisan base of support.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral on March 25, 1999, and never reported it out or scheduled a markup.

against.name: House Education and the Workforce Committee and House Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral; the Commerce bill was sent to subcommittees in April 1999 and never advanced further.

against.name: National Rifle Association and firearms industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal child-access and gun-design mandates of this kind, and the bill's dealer regulation, during the 106th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was heavily Democratic — 55 Democrats to 6 Republicans — and no committee ever took the bill up, so it never reached a vote on which a party split could be measured.

industries.note: The bill would have required redesign of most semiautomatic pistols (magazine disconnect safeties) and triggered drop-testing requirements, creating compliance costs for manufacturers. The industry's interest ran against the bill's child-safety rules, though the bill preserved liability actions against manufacturers [S3].

Dealers faced mandatory security standards, annual inspections, license revocation for willful sales to minors, and added ID requirements for young buyers. Dealers' interest in avoiding these requirements ran against the bill's enforcement goals [S3].

industries.industry: State health departments and law enforcement agencies
industries.note: The bill authorized roughly $5 million per year for state child firearm injury surveillance and expanded federal tracing grants, so agencies would have received funding rather than bearing costs [S3].
